hints: Focus on what a catalyst actually changes, the reaction pathway, not the energy of the particles themselves.
Remember the curve shape depends only on temperature, so at room temperature the distribution of energies stays exactly the same.
Think about what happens to the area to the right of $E_a$ if the $E_a$ line moves to a lower energy value.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the diagram shows**

Think of the curve as showing how energy is shared out between the Q particles at room temperature. Only the few particles to the right of $E_a$ have enough energy to decompose when they collide.

$$Q(g) \rightarrow X(g) + Z(g)$$

**Recall what a catalyst does**

A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy. It does not heat the particles up or give them more kinetic energy.

$$E_{a(catalysed)} < E_{a(uncatalysed)}$$

**Apply this to the Boltzmann curve**

Because temperature is unchanged, the curve itself does not move or change shape. The $E_a$ line moves to the left to a lower energy value, so a much larger area is now to the right of $E_a$. That means many more particles can now react.

options.A: Incorrect. The peak position and shape of the Boltzmann distribution depend on temperature. Adding a catalyst at the same room temperature leaves the curve unchanged, so the peak does not move.
options.B: Correct. A catalyst lowers $E_a$, so the $E_a$ mark moves left. The fraction of particles with energy $\ge E_a$ (the area under the curve to the right of $E_a$) gets bigger, so more Q particles can decompose.
options.C: Incorrect. A catalyst does not increase particle kinetic energy or temperature. Average kinetic energy stays the same, only the energy barrier is lowered.
options.D: Incorrect. It is true that $E_a$ decreases, but a smaller $E_a$ value means the dotted line moves to the left (toward the origin), not to the right. This is a common direction trap.
